extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, translators, and literary critics / educated readers of Romantic-era literature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and prescriptive comments on poetry, drama, translation, and versification drawn from a Romantic-era literary-criticism text (travel/letters + Biographia Literaria material). Emphasizes what constitutes good verse, drama, translation fidelity, plotting, and poetic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious blank verse (versification)
rubrics_metrics.description: “harmonious verse (the English iambic blank verse above all) consists in the apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs, and not in the even flow, much less in the prominence or antithetic vigour, of single lines”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange pauses and cadences to create paragraph-long sweeps; single lines should only be prominent when intentionally introduced for a specific purpose. Avoid an even, monotonous flow; seek larger structural cadences rather than isolated line effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's aim: elevate rather than descend
rubrics_metrics.description: “it was the province of a great poet to raise people up to his own level, not to descend to theirs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects and techniques that invite readers to a higher imaginative or moral plane rather than pandering to common tastes; resist lowering art to mere popular gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing long poems on mere appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: “it was unworthy of a man of genius to make the interest of a long poem turn entirely upon animal gratification.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain long-form poetry by varied intellectual, moral, and imaginative resources, not by repeated appeals to sensual or appetitive stimuli; avoid prolonged reliance on erotic or purely bodily interest to hold attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity in translation (no additions/omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of English translations of the Messiah: “the English was no translation — there were pages on pages not in the original : — and half the original was not to be found in the translation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should avoid inserting new material or omitting substantial portions of the source. Maintain fidelity to the original's scope and content; beware translators who add or excise passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the native idiom of the target language
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that borrowing foreign idioms can injure style: “Milton had often injured both his prose and verse by taking this liberty too frequently. I recommended to him the prose works of Dryden as models of pure and native English.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the natural idiom and idiomatic resources of the target language; avoid forcing source-language turns of phrase that distort native expression. Use exemplary native writers as models for purity of idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic excellence: essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their deficiency is in depth and in imagination: their excellence is in the construction of the plot; the good sense of the sentiments; the sobriety of the morals, and the high polish of the diction and dialogue.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramas by their plot construction, soundness of sentiment, moral sobriety, and polished diction/dialogue. Depth and imagination are desirable but the fundamentals listed are core measures of dramatic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant, improbable melodrama
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of popular German/romantic drama: use of ‘horrific incidents and mysterious villains… ruined castles, dungeons, trap-doors, skeletons, the perpetual moonshine’ and a ‘bloated style’ and ‘morbid consciousness’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of contrived supernatural gadgets, overblown sensational incidents, and morbid sentimentalism that substitute spectacle for plausible character and plot; prefer credible imaginative invention over mechanical Gothic tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap sentimental manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: On tragedy and audience: “nothing was more easy than to deluge an audience — that it was done every day by the meanest writers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on easy devices to produce tears or mass emotional reaction; strive for artful pathos grounded in character and truth rather than melodramatic tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character intelligibility, even for ideal/supernatural figures
rubrics_metrics.description: On Don Juan: “Don Juan is, from beginning to end, an intelligible character: as much so as the Satan of Milton. The poet asks only of the reader what as a poet he is privileged to ask, viz., that sort of negative faith in the existence of such a being.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a character is idealized, mythic, or supernatural, they must be coherent and intelligible within the poem/drama’s internal logic. Readers can accept unreal beings, but those beings must be psychologically and narratively consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan thoroughly before composition; compose in favourable moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographical note on composition: the poet “devoted three entire years to the plan without composing a single line… he composed no more in prose… he only composed in favourable moments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a detailed plan for large poetic works before drafting; rely on concentrated, inspired composing moments rather than continuous forced output. Long works benefit from a completed scheme and episodic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive, skillful borrowing from sources (tasteful theft)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Wieland and older romance writers: he regarded their books and fables ‘in the light of the ancient mythology, as a sort of common property, from which a man was free to take whatever he could make a good use of.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing from older or foreign sources can be legitimate if done artfully and with good judgment; treat common cultural materials as resources to be transformed, not slavishly copied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about cross-language line equivalence and meter
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of translation of heroic lines: Klopstock claimed a German line could always equal a Greek/Latin line; reply: ‘in English we could commonly render one Greek heroic line in a line and a half… this line and a half would be found to contain no more syllables than one German or Greek hexameter.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume one-to-one line equivalence across languages; consider differences in meter, syllable counts, and idiomatic compression. Translators should account for metrical and rhythmic disparities rather than asserting literal line parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different practices for rhyme and final endings across languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: “we were not so exact with regard to the final endings of lines as the French… He did not seem to know that we made no distinction between masculine and feminine (i.e. single or double) rhymes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of national/rhetorical differences (e.g., French strictness about final endings, distinctions between masculine/feminine rhymes); adapt expectations and technique to the conventions of the language you are writing in.
